name: Mistletoe extract

lead: Mistletoe extract comes from European mistletoe (Viscum album). It appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products, where it is used for soothing and a healthier-looking complexion.

The chain claimed is soothing and antioxidant action on the skin. Mistletoe's published human research is in cancer care: injectable extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary treatments, and mistletoe lectins have been reported to stimulate immune signalling. No study of mistletoe on skin or appearance was identified.

paras: In skincare it is used as one botanical among others in creams, serums and essences within a daily routine. Medicinal injectable extracts are a separate use, administered in clinical settings.

The plant contains the toxin viscumin, which works by a mechanism similar to ricin; European mistletoe is described as more toxic than American mistletoe. Topical cosmetic safety was not covered in the reviewed sources, and the plant is not meant to be eaten.

angle.text: Mistletoe extract appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare, used for soothing and healthier-looking skin. Its published research is in complementary cancer care, with immune-signalling effects reported for its lectins.

lead: Mistletoe extract is prepared from European mistletoe (Viscum album), a hemiparasitic evergreen shrub that grows on the branches of host trees.[1] Standardised or proprietary extracts such as Iscador, Helixor and abnobaVISCUM are used as complementary cancer treatments, mainly in German-speaking countries, and the plant also appears as a botanical ingredient in some Korean-style skincare products, where it is included for a soothing, plant-derived image.[2][3][4]

The plant's toxins include viscumin, which inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis by a mechanism similar to ricin's; European mistletoe is described as more toxic than American mistletoe.[5] Medicinal extracts contain mistletoe lectins that have been studied for immune-stimulating effects.[3][6]

Published human research concerns cancer patients, not skin. No study of mistletoe extract on skin or appearance has been published; for someone interested in the skincare use, the relevant background is the plant's lectin chemistry and its use as an injectable adjunct in cancer care.
infobox: Injectable prescription extracts, widely used in German-speaking countries[4]
Injectable mistletoe not commercially available or approved for cancer; listed in the Homeopathic Pharmacopoeia[4]

paras: Viscum album has leathery, yellowish-green leaves in opposite pairs and white or yellow berries. It grows on broad-leaved trees such as apple, lime, hawthorn and poplar and is native to Europe and western and southern Asia.[1] Product composition varies with the host tree, harvest time, preparation method and manufacturer, and some preparations are homeopathic and not chemically standardised.[4]

Mistletoe has a long place in folklore: Pliny the Elder described Celtic druids harvesting it with ceremony, it features in Greek and Roman myth and in Norse legend, and kissing under mistletoe at Christmas is first documented in 16th-century England.[1] As a medicine, it has been used in traditional and folk practice for conditions including cancer, epilepsy and hypertension, and the NCI summary dates modern interest in it as an anticancer treatment to the 1920s, with most clinical studies published in German.[4]

Wikipedia states that the use of mistletoe extract in cancer treatment originated with Rudolf Steiner, founder of anthroposophy.[1] Anthroposophic medicine, including Iscador, remains the best-known tradition of mistletoe therapy.

A 1989 study reported that the beta-galactoside-specific lectin from Iscador had immunomodulatory effects in rabbits and patients.[3] A 1990 study reported that the lectin increased secretion of tumour necrosis factor alpha and interleukins 1 and 6 by human mononuclear cells.[6] The lectin's ligand-binding characteristics have also been characterised.[7]

A phase I trial in 15 healthy male volunteers described the pharmacokinetics of natural mistletoe lectins after subcutaneous injection.[8] Laboratory work has reported that mistletoe-extract drugs stimulate anti-cancer Vgamma9Vdelta2 T cells,[9] and a zebrafish study reported a radioprotective effect on intestinal toxicity.[10] A review has proposed that mistletoe therapy could be used to stimulate the innate immune system, drawing a parallel to the bacterial extracts of William Coley.[11]

In Europe, mistletoe extracts are widely used and marketed as injectable prescription drugs, particularly in German-speaking countries. In the United States, these injectable products are not commercially available and are not approved to treat cancer, although Viscum album is listed in the Homeopathic Pharmacopoeia of the United States.[4]

Mistletoe extract is listed as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products.[2] The research literature on the plant does not include skin or cosmetic trials, so formulation claims are not backed by published studies of this ingredient on skin.

Wikipedia describes viscumin as toxic, notes that concentrated forms such as herbal tea can be potentially fatal and that eating the berries has caused serious illness.[5][1] The NCI summary says mistletoe plants and berries are considered poisonous, while few serious side effects have been linked to extract use.[4] Topical cosmetic safety has not been reviewed in the published literature.

Human studies relate to cancer. The EORTC 18871/DKG 80-1 phase III melanoma trial included an Iscador M arm alongside interferon arms and an observation group.[12] A randomised trial in China examined quality of life with a standardised extract in breast, ovarian and lung cancer,[13] and a placebo-controlled trial reported improved quality of life in breast cancer patients during chemotherapy with extract PS76A2.[14] A randomised trial examined quality of life in advanced pancreatic cancer,[15] and a 2009 systematic review examined survival in patients given Iscador.[16] A trial in resected head and neck cancer has also been published.[17]

More recent work includes a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of survival with non-fermented extract,[18] a 2023 analysis of how mistletoe is prescribed across clinical studies, which described the topic as discussed controversially as a complementary treatment,[19] a phase I trial of intravenous Helixor M in advanced cancer, which noted that use is controversial because of suboptimal trials,[20] and the double-blind placebo-controlled MISTRAL trial in advanced pancreatic cancer.[21] The NCI summary says many studies reported improved survival or quality of life but that many had major weaknesses, and that mistletoe should not be recommended outside well-designed trials.[4] No trial examined skin or cosmetic outcomes.

timeline.event: Modern interest in mistletoe as an anticancer treatment begins.[4]
Study reports immunomodulatory effects of the Iscador lectin.[3]
EORTC phase III melanoma trial results published.[12]
Randomised trial of quality of life in advanced pancreatic cancer published.[15]
MISTRAL double-blind trial in advanced pancreatic cancer published.[21]
